blocks.text: It is proved that שפן saphan is not the rabbit, as they maintain, but a kind of larger mouse in Eretz Yisrael, Egypt, and Libya, which by Herodotus and others is called Δίπους [Dipous], by the Elders Χοιρογρύλλιος [Choirogryllios], by Jerome Ἀρκτομῦς [Arktomys], and by the Arabs اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo, concerning which many things, not yet published, are brought forth from the writings of the Arabs.

In Levit, XI, 5. and Deut. XIV, 7. among those animals that indeed chew the cud, [col. 1002] yet do not have a cloven hoof, and are therefore unclean, along with the camel and the hare is listed השפן, ὁ σαφάν [ho saphan]. The plural שפנים sephanim is found in Psal. CIV. 18. The rock is a refuge לשפנים, τοῖς σεφανίμ [tois sephanim]. And in Prov. XXX, 26. שפנים sephanim are a feeble folk, yet they make their home in the rock. Most of the more recent scholars explain them as rabbits. Which interpretation many things seem to favor on the surface. 1. Because twice in the Law השפן is joined with הארנבת, that is, with the hare, as an animal of the same kind. 2. Because the passage of the Psalm which we have just cited is rendered thus in the Greek edition: Πέτρα καταφυγὴ τοῖς λαγωοῖς [Petra kataphygē tois lagōois], The rock is a refuge for the hares. Certain copies have τοῖς χοιρογρυλλίοις [tois choirogrylliois], that is, as they maintain, for the hedgehogs. But the oldest writers follow the former reading. Jerome, in Epistle 135 to Sunia and Fretela: All translated it with a similar word, χοιρογρυλλίους [choirogryllious]: only the LXX rendered it hares. So also read Theodoret in his Commentary on this Psalm, Basil on Isaiah chapter 2, and Apollinaris in his Paraphrase,
Πέτροις ἠλιβάτοις περιθάρσεες εἰσὶ λαγωοὶ [Petrois ēlibatois peritharsees eisi lagōoi],

Trusting in steep rocks are the hares: and the Arabic version, which was translated from the Greek, The rocks are a refuge الارانب [al-arānib] of hares. Others join both: as Augustine on this passage, The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs and hares. Arnobius, There is the rock, affording a refuge either to the young of hedgehogs, etc. or to hares. Bede on Proverbs chapter 30, And it is to be noted that in the Psalm, where we sing: “The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs, in some codices is found for hares, in some for choerogryllii”. 3. The Hebrew of Prov. XXX, 26. שפנים עם לא עצום, the Vulgate translator rendered thus, The little hare, a feeble folk, having followed, if I am not mistaken, [II, 410] some Greek translator who had explained שפנים as λαγίδεις [lagideis], little hares, that is, rabbits. For thus in Strabo, book 3, λαγίδεις [lagideis], little hares, are taken for rabbits. The Greeks have no other name for the rabbit. For in Aelian κόνιλος [konilos], in Polybius and Galen κούνικλος [kouniklos], were proper words of the Spaniards, and in Strabo and Erotian λεβηρὶς [lebēris] of the Massilians, not used in Greece. 4. The ancient Book of Names, which they ascribe to Philo, has it thus on Jeremiah: SAPHAN, choerogryllius, hare, or hedgehog. And on Ezekiel: SAPHAN, hedgehog, or hare. 5. In the Arabic Lexicon of Giggeius, p. 854, vol. 2, سفن [sfn] saphan is rendered rabbit. Where he got this from, however, I do not know at all. For I have found it nowhere else. 6. The Hebrew name שפן saphan seems to allude to the Hebrew verbs ספן and צפן, of which the former signifies to cover, the latter to hide. And it seems to fit the rabbit, which seeks the hiding places of burrows in order to lie hid in them and, so to speak, be covered over. Martial:
The rabbit delights to dwell in hollowed-out caves.
